question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on on an Alabama lake, what is each operator required to do?
choice_a: Neither vessel needs to alter course; they should hold their exact heading
choice_b: Both vessels should turn to port (left) and pass starboard-to-starboard
choice_c: Each vessel should alter course to starboard (right) so they pass port-to-port, keeping right as if meeting oncoming traffic on a road
choice_d: Whichever vessel is faster has the right to choose which side to pass on
explanation: In a head-on meeting situation, the Navigation Rules require each power-driven vessel to alter course to starboard so the two vessels pass port side to port side, just as vehicles keep to the right on a two-way road.
source_note: ALEA boating rules and regulations ("rules of the road"); Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 14 (head-on situation)

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels on Alabama waters, which vessel must yield?
choice_a: Neither vessel is required to yield; both may proceed on the same course
choice_b: The larger of the two vessels always has the right of way regardless of position
choice_c: The faster vessel always has the right of way
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching on its own starboard (right) side must give way and yield to the vessel on its right
explanation: When two power-driven vessels are crossing so as to involve risk of collision, the vessel that has the other on its own starboard side is the give-way vessel and must yield, while the other becomes the stand-on vessel and generally maintains course and speed.
source_note: ALEA boating rules and regulations; Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 15 (crossing situation)

question: Under the Navigation Rules, what must an overtaking vessel do when passing a slower vessel ahead of it on Alabama waters?
choice_a: The overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, regardless of which side it passes on, until it is well clear
choice_b: The vessel being overtaken must always get out of the way of the faster vessel behind it
choice_c: Overtaking is prohibited everywhere in Alabama
choice_d: The overtaking vessel may pass at any speed with no wake restriction
explanation: The vessel doing the overtaking is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken until safely past and clear, regardless of which side the pass occurs on -- and Alabama's speed rules still require reducing speed to avoid a hazardous wake near the other vessel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 13 (overtaking); ALEA boating rules and regulations (hazardous wake requirement)

question: Under the general priority hierarchy of the Navigation Rules, which vessel generally has the right of way over a power-driven vessel operating under engine power alone?
choice_a: A power-driven vessel always outranks every sailing vessel
choice_b: A sailing vessel under sail alone, as well as vessels that are less maneuverable, such as one restricted in its ability to maneuver or not under command
choice_c: The larger power-driven vessel always outranks the smaller
choice_d: No vessel type ever outranks another; right-of-way is decided purely by which one arrives first
explanation: The Navigation Rules establish a hierarchy where less maneuverable vessels generally have priority: a vessel not under command, one restricted in its ability to maneuver, and a sailing vessel under sail alone generally rank above an ordinary power-driven vessel, which must keep clear of them.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 18 (responsibilities between vessels)

question: On the Gulf Intracoastal Waterway through Mobile Bay, why must a small recreational boat give a wide berth to a commercial tug pushing a barge?
choice_a: Tugs and barges are not required to follow any right-of-way rules
choice_b: Because commercial vessels always have lower priority than recreational boats under the Navigation Rules
choice_c: Because a tug and tow are considered restricted in their ability to maneuver, cannot stop or turn quickly, and often cannot see small boats close ahead of them
choice_d: There is no special caution needed since barges move slower than recreational boats
explanation: A tug pushing or towing a barge has very limited maneuverability, long stopping distances, and significant blind spots close to the bow of the tow -- recreational boaters on Mobile Bay's Intracoastal Waterway segment should stay well clear rather than assume the tug can react quickly.
source_note: Universal Navigation Rules vessel-priority principles applied to Alabama's Gulf Intracoastal Waterway commercial traffic

question: What general speed and wake rule does Alabama impose when a vessel approaches other vessels, harbor areas, or a shoreline?
choice_a: Wake is never a legal concern in Alabama
choice_b: Full speed is always permitted regardless of proximity to other vessels or the shoreline
choice_c: Speed limits only apply on the Gulf of Mexico, not on inland lakes
choice_d: Operators must reduce speed to avoid creating a hazardous wake and must operate at a speed that is reasonable and prudent for the conditions
explanation: Alabama's boating rules require operators to reduce speed near other vessels and harbor areas to avoid producing a hazardous wake, and more generally to operate at a speed that is reasonable and prudent given the traffic, weather, and visibility conditions present.
source_note: ALEA boating rules and regulations (speed and wake requirement)

question: What unusual right-of-way rule does Alabama boating law state regarding aircraft?
choice_a: No vessel shall obstruct or interfere with the take-off, landing, or taxiing of an aircraft
choice_b: Vessels always have the right of way over any aircraft operating on the water
choice_c: Aircraft are banned from operating on any Alabama waterway
choice_d: Alabama law does not address aircraft on the water in any way
explanation: Alabama's boating regulations specifically state that no vessel may obstruct or interfere with an aircraft's take-off, landing, or taxiing, which matters on waters near seaplane bases and along the Gulf Coast and larger lakes where floatplanes may operate.
source_note: ALEA boating rules and regulations (aircraft interference prohibition)

question: What is a "stand-on vessel" under the Navigation Rules, and what is it generally required to do?
choice_a: The vessel that must always come to a complete stop whenever another vessel is nearby
choice_b: The vessel with right-of-way in a given encounter, which should generally maintain its course and speed so the give-way vessel can safely maneuver around it
choice_c: A vessel that is anchored and not moving at all
choice_d: A vessel with mechanical problems that cannot get underway
explanation: The stand-on vessel is the one with right-of-way in a meeting, crossing, or overtaking situation and is expected to hold its course and speed so the give-way vessel can take early, obvious action to keep clear -- though the stand-on vessel must still act to avoid collision if the give-way vessel fails to do so.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 17 (action by stand-on vessel)

question: What must every vessel operator on Alabama waters maintain at all times under the Navigation Rules, regardless of right-of-way status?
choice_a: No lookout is required if the operator has radar
choice_b: A constant radio broadcast announcing the vessel's position
choice_c: A proper lookout by sight and hearing to fully assess the risk of collision
choice_d: A lookout is only required at night
explanation: Every vessel must maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times, using all available means appropriate to the circumstances, so the operator can fully assess the risk of collision -- a duty that applies regardless of which vessel technically has the right of way.

question: On Lake Guntersville, a fishing boat under power meets a sailboat under sail alone, with risk of collision. Who must give way?
choice_a: Whichever vessel is closest to shore has the right of way
choice_b: The sailboat, because sailing vessels must always yield to power-driven vessels
choice_c: Neither vessel needs to take any action
choice_d: The fishing boat, because a sailing vessel under sail alone generally outranks an ordinary power-driven vessel in the Navigation Rules' priority hierarchy
explanation: Under the Navigation Rules' general priority hierarchy, a sailing vessel operating under sail alone ranks above an ordinary power-driven vessel, so the power-driven fishing boat is the give-way vessel and must take early action to avoid the sailboat.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules, Rule 18 (responsibilities between vessels)
